judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the required 'Enquiry Phone Number*' input in the HubSpot customer service form, with the visible description 'Best contact number for this enquiry'. claimTrue: in the snapshot it is type="text" inputmode="text" with no autocomplete attribute, while its sibling fields First name, Last name and Email do carry given-name, family-name and email. It asks for the enquirer's own contact number, so it collects information about the user, and 'tel' is a listed input purpose. I looked for a reason it could pass: the field is visible in the screenshot, it is not inside an iframe, and there is no other phone field with autocomplete="tel". Understanding 1.3.5 says that type alone is too broad and that browser heuristics do not meet the criterion, so even a phone-number type would not cure it. captureDiffers: the form is built client-side, so I fetched its live HubSpot definition (portal 26166057, the same form id). It still has enquiry_phone_number as a required phonenumber field with the same description. I also checked HubSpot's live v2 embed script, which sets autocomplete only for known contact properties such as phone and mobilephone (tel), firstname and lastname. For any other name it returns nothing, so every browser gets this ticket property without autocomplete, the same as the capture. I found no reason that holds up, so the field fails 1.3.5 as the claim says.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the 'Email address' input of the footer newsletter sign-up ('Never miss a show ... Sign up'), and it asks for the visitor's own email address. claimTrue: the snapshot shows type="email" name="email" with no autocomplete attribute. Its formIssues list holds Chromium's FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError, so the claim that Chromium's form check flags it is also true of the capture. Skeptic checks: the only hints of purpose are type="email" and name="email". Understanding 1.3.5 says outright that type="email" 'does not clarify if the purpose is for entering the user's email address or some other person's email', and that browser heuristics are 'not sufficient to meet the requirements of this criterion'. H98 (autocomplete) is the sufficient technique, and it is not used here. captureDiffers: the live page's server-rendered HTML, fetched today, has the same input markup with no autocomplete, so it matches the capture. The dimming in the screenshot comes from the cookie banner and does not affect this claim. I found no reason that holds up, so the field fails 1.3.5 as the claim says.
